etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English blody, blodi, from Old English blōdiġ, blōdeġ (“bloody”), from Proto-West Germanic *blōdag, from Proto-Germanic *blōþagaz (“bloody”), equivalent to blood +‎ -y. Cognate with Dutch bloedig (“bloody”), German blutig (“bloody”), Danish blodig (“bloody”), Swedish blodig (“bloody”), Icelandic blóðugur (“bloody”). See Wikipedia for thoughts on sense evolution.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “A Midsommer Nights Dreame”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: And, as she fled, her mantle she did fall, / Which Lion vile with bloody mouth did stain.

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i], page 119:
quote.text: O Antony! Begge not your death of vs: / Though now we muſt appeare bloody and cruell, / As by our hands, and this our preſent Acte / You ſee we do: Yet ſee you but our hands, / And this, the bleeding buſineſſe they haue done:

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene ii], page 336:
quote.text: Some bloody paſſion ſhakes your very Frame:

quote.citation: 1846 [1845], Frederick Douglass, chapter I, in Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave, Boston: Anti-Slavery Office, page 8:
quote.text: I had therefore been, until now, out of the way of the bloody scenes that often occurred on the plantation.

quote.citation: 2007, Lucinda Mallows, Lucy Mallows, Slovakia: The Bradt Travel Guide, page 169:
quote.text: The story of Elizabeth Bathory is one of the bloodiest in history.

definitions.definition: (informal, British, Ireland, Commonwealth, Hawaii, mildly vulgar) Used as an intensifier.

quote.citation: 1916 May 31, David Beatty during the Battle of Jutland:
quote.text: There seems to be something wrong with our bloody ships today.

quote.citation: 1994, Robert Jordan, Lord of Chaos, page 519:
quote.text: Try to keep those bloody women's bloody heads on their bloody shoulders by somehow helping them make this whole mad impossible scheme actually work.

quote.citation: 2003, Mark Haddon, The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time, page 64:
quote.text: You are not to go asking anyone about who killed that bloody dog.

quote.citation: 2007, James MacFarlane, Avenge My Kin, Book 2: A Time of Testing, page 498
quote.text: “You bloody fool, I could′ve stabbed you in the heart,” David said in mock anger, and then smiled widely.

quote.citation: 2024 January 24, Dyan Perry talks to Nick Brodrick, “The industry has given me so much”, in RAIL, number 1001, page 45:
quote.text: With 109km of fixed infrastructure, of which only 50% is utilised, Perry's message is simple: "put more bloody trains on it!"

quote.citation: 1945, Evelyn Waugh, chapter 5, in Brideshead Revisited […], 3rd edition, London: Chapman & Hall, →OCLC, book 1 (Et in Arcadia Ego), pages 118–119:
quote.text: Come to apologize to Charles. I was bloody to him and he's my guest. He's my guest and my only friend and I was bloody to him.

definitions.definition: (informal, Australia, British, India, Ireland, Newfoundland, New Zealand, South Africa, mildly vulgar) Used to express anger, annoyance, or shock, or for emphasis.

quote.citation: 1912 (date written), [George] Bernard Shaw, “Pygmalion”, in Androcles and the Lion, Overruled, Pygmalion, London: Constable and Company, published 1916, →OCLC, Act III, page 153:
quote.text: Walk! Not bloody likely. [Sensation]. I am going in a taxi. [She goes out].

quote.citation: 1994, Robert Jordan, Lord of Chaos, page 109:
quote.text: "Dice are no bloody good," David said.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To draw blood from (one's opponent) in a fight.
(transitive) To demonstrably harm (the cause of an opponent). (Can we add an example for this sense?)
